title: Good Data, Bad Data
outcome: By the end, I can repair data with traceable evidence while preserving valid zero and unknown.
scenario: A fictional toy-car distance table needs cleaning before use.
given: Contract: unique run ID; whole distance 0–30 cm. Raw rows: A=0 cm, B=200 mm, C=blank, another A=0 cm.
Source log confirms one A run and B’s original measurement of 200 mm; C has no measurement.

steps.label: Validate rows
steps.detail: A’s zero is valid; B has wrong unit; C is missing; A is duplicated.

steps.label: Evidence repair
steps.detail: 200 mm ÷10 =20 cm; source log supports retaining one A.

steps.label: Keep unknown
steps.detail: C stays unresolved; do not replace it with 0.

steps.label: Clean record
steps.detail: Usable unique rows: A=0 cm, B=20 cm; retain a separate change log.

explanation: Cleaning is not permission to make inconvenient values plausible. The source log supports a unit conversion and removal of a duplicate copy. Zero means a measured zero distance; blank means no supplied measurement. Keep the raw table and explain every change so someone can reconstruct what happened.

counterfactual.change: The source log gives B only as bare 200 with no unit.
counterfactual.prediction: B remains unresolved rather than becoming 20 cm.
counterfactual.reason: Without a confirmed unit, division by 10 would be an unsupported assumption.

student_task: Which repairs are evidence-backed in the original case, and which row must remain unknown?
teacher_answer: Convert B to 20 cm and keep one confirmed A; C stays unknown. A’s valid zero must not be treated as missing.
project_evidence: Keep raw sorter inputs, validated records and an evidence-linked repair log as different artifacts.
limits: A clean table can still contain measurement or labelling errors that these checks do not detect.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
